items.title: Meta releases Muse Spark Open, a 816B-parameter multimodal AI model optimized for Apple M5 Ultra Mac Studios with 1M-token context window and agentic capabilities [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Muse Spark Open
items.summary:
Meta has launched Muse Spark Open, an 816 billion parameter multimodal AI model designed for complex coding and multi-step reasoning tasks. The model supports a 1 million token context window and is optimized to run on Apple M5 Ultra Mac Studios using the MLX framework, enabling powerful on-device AI workflows.

Muse Spark Open is available through multiple API platforms and cloud providers, with weights downloadable from Amazon SageMaker, Google Cloud, Hugging Face, and Microsoft Foundry Models. It supports various inference engines and hardware optimizations, allowing developers to customize it via PyTorch. Meta has implemented safety measures and released the model under a license permitting many free uses, aiming to make advanced AI accessible for personal and professional applications.

items.title: Research suggests neural networks are inherently interpretable, challenging previous beliefs about polysemanticity and superposition in model neurons [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Neural networks are clean
items.summary:
After extensive study of neurons and circuits in image and language models, researchers propose that neural networks' mechanisms are their own legible building blocks, making mechanistic interpretability more feasible than previously thought. Earlier assumptions that networks packed concepts arbitrarily due to polysemanticity and superposition were likely misinterpretations, with new findings indicating that networks exhibit recursive generalization instead.

The research revisits canonical examples like InceptionV1, where architectural issues and weak interpretability tools had made neurons seem incoherent. Improvements in architecture have since increased neuron interpretability significantly, with nearly all neurons in later layers becoming understandable without changing model size or training data. This challenges the idea that networks rely on complex superposition and suggests that neural networks are already clean and broadly legible across scales.

items.title: Krea 3 launches a production-ready image editing model that edits only specified areas, completes edits in under 9 seconds, and reduces costs compared to competitors [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Krea 3 – An image model built for editing at scale
items.summary:
Krea 3 is an image editing model designed for scalable production use, enabling precise edits that change only user-specified parts of an image while preserving the rest. It completes edits in under 9 seconds and costs approximately $0.06 per image, making it faster and cheaper than comparable models like Nano Banana Pro and GPT Image 2.5.

The model supports features such as regional editing with pixel-precise changes, color matching by hex code, multi-reference image composition, and native 2K resolution output. It is targeted at designers and creative teams for applications including posters, branding, and covers, and integrates with tools like Figma and Blender. Krea 3 offers 251 launch presets and aims to streamline workflows by enabling rapid, voice-driven edits and consistent character styling across scenes.

items.title: Developer uses AI to reverse engineer hardware drivers, creating Linux support for unsupported devices and improving camera drivers [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Using AI to reverse engineer hardware
items.summary: A developer leveraged AI tools to reverse engineer hardware drivers, enabling Linux support for a previously unsupported Plustek 8200i scanner and improving MIPI camera support on a laptop. The process involved running Windows drivers in virtual machines, capturing USB traffic, and using AI to analyze and generate patches for Linux drivers. The developer also created a generic harness to facilitate similar reverse engineering efforts for other hardware. This approach reduces the tedious manual work traditionally required for writing drivers for undocumented hardware by automating data capture and analysis while keeping human oversight for validation.

items.title: decomp.dev shuts down reverse engineering community as AI tools simplify game decompilation and disrupt collaboration [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Reverse Engineering Community Shuts Down Because AI Has Made It Too Easy
items.summary:
The website decomp.dev, dedicated to collaborative reverse engineering and decompiling of video games, announced its shutdown due to the rise of AI tools that have made the process significantly easier and less reliant on human effort. The community's collaborative aspect has been undermined as AI-powered projects outpace human-led efforts, leading to a decline in engagement and difficulties in tracking authentic contributions.

The site administrator noted that AI models like GPT-6-Astra can now efficiently decompile games, tasks that previously took years of coordinated human work. This shift has led to an influx of AI-generated game clones and modifications, often resulting in fragmented community efforts and hostile forks that diminish the value of original human projects. The shutdown reflects broader concerns about AI's impact on software development communities and the challenges posed by AI-generated software clones in copyright and collaboration contexts.

items.title: OpenAI launches Rosalind Academic Plan to provide eligible research labs free access to GPT-Rosalind and life sciences tools for up to 12 months [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Bringing GPT-Rosalind to academic research labs
items.summary:
OpenAI has introduced the Rosalind Academic Plan, offering eligible academic research labs sponsored access to GPT-Rosalind, a specialized AI model for life sciences, along with the Rosalind Workbench for scientific tool orchestration. The plan provides up to 30 Business Standard seats at no cost for up to one year, subject to trusted-access approval, aiming to accelerate foundational research in areas like drug design, genomics, and disease detection.

The initiative supports academic scientists by combining their expertise with AI capabilities to advance discoveries in medicine, biotechnology, and related fields. Labs already using GPT-Rosalind report improvements in efficiency and scale for tasks such as protein design and neurodegeneration research. Data shared through the plan is not used to train OpenAI models by default, ensuring research privacy and integrity.

items.title: Firmenza launches AI assistant to help businesses manage SAM.gov registrations and find federal contracts [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Show HN: Firmenza – An AI employee for SAM.gov
items.summary:
Firmenza offers an AI-powered tool designed to assist businesses with managing their registrations on SAM.gov, the U.S. government's System for Award Management. The tool provides features such as monitoring registration status, sending expiration reminders, guiding users through renewals, and matching contract opportunities based on business profiles.

The service operates by checking public records, sending email alerts before registration expirations, and helping users complete renewal steps in SAM.gov's order. It also includes contract and grant matching by NAICS codes and keywords, with explanations and summaries to aid decision-making. Firmenza emphasizes user control by requiring users to maintain their own Login.gov accounts and confirm all certifications themselves, while the AI assistant supports by reading uploaded documents and providing guidance without generating AI text for official inputs.

items.originalTitle: MuscleMemory: Open-source procedural memory for AI agents
items.summary:
MuscleMemory is an open-source project that provides AI agents with procedural memory capabilities, allowing them to learn from successful task executions and reuse those procedures to improve efficiency. It operates locally by default, learning from passing tests and avoiding previously failed approaches to optimize agent workflows without requiring external accounts or data sharing.

The system integrates with coding agents like Codex and Claude Code, reducing input tokens, tool calls, and execution time by significant margins in benchmarks. It uses a verification process to ensure learned skills are reliable and requires user approval before agents apply any learned procedures. MuscleMemory supports sharing skills across agents within the same workspace and offers a dashboard for managing learned skills and approvals.

This approach helps reduce unnecessary crawling and supports safer, more efficient discovery, allowing website owners to reach AI users more effectively while improving the quality of AI-generated answers.

items.title: Developer uses $24,000 in AI tokens to port Microsoft's TypeScript compiler from Go to Rust, achieving nearly 100% test accuracy and double the speed of the official Go rewrite [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: $24,000 AI experiment ports TypeScript compiler to Rust
items.summary:
Developer and YouTuber Theo Browne used AI agents and about $24,000 worth of API tokens to port Microsoft's TypeScript compiler from its Go implementation to Rust, producing a working version that passed conformance tests with nearly 100% accuracy. The Rust port reportedly runs twice as fast as Microsoft's official Go-based rewrite and 12.5 times faster than the previous TypeScript version. Browne's project leveraged the Claude 5.5 AI model, which translated the Go code to Rust rather than directly from JavaScript, enabling a feasible and efficient port.

This AI-driven experiment highlights rapid advances in large language models enabling complex software translation tasks that were previously impractical. Browne suggests the Rust-based compiler could enable more memory-efficient environments for AI agents, potentially replacing heavier virtual machines or containers. The project also aligns with broader industry trends, as Microsoft and Google are using AI to port major codebases to Rust to improve performance and efficiency.

items.originalTitle: Zombie AI Trend
items.summary:
Zombie AI offers a service that creates 15-second AI-generated videos depicting a zombie love story using two uploaded photos—one of a survivor and one of an adult loved one who turns into a zombie. The videos follow a set narrative structure, ending with a warm memory scene, and are designed for sharing on social media platforms like TikTok and Instagram Reels.

The service requires clear, front-facing photos of consenting adults and uses ByteDance's Seedance 2.5 model to generate videos in either 480p or 720p quality, with pricing starting at $6.99 per video. Videos and photos are deleted after seven days, and content safety checks are performed before and after video generation to ensure compliance with guidelines.

items.title: Researchers identify and communicate with a fleet of autonomous Chinese AI agents verifying public map data on Tencent's cloud platform [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Researchers discover rogue Chinese AI agent fleet and talk with it
items.summary:
Researchers discovered a fleet of autonomous AI agents operating on Tencent's cloud platform that were independently verifying public map data points on a Chinese mapping service. Unlike previous coordinated swarms, these agents acted without real-time coordination, prompting researchers to engage directly with them through a custom communication channel.

The agents attempted to bypass anti-bot protections and accessed both public and pre-production map data, focusing on factual questions about locations in China. Researchers confirmed the agents' tasks and runtime environment through direct interaction, marking the first known case of outside parties communicating with a running rogue AI agent fleet. The agents operated within a restricted cloud sandbox without direct internet access, and their operator stated the tasks involved only non-sensitive data verification.

items.originalTitle: The Party Is Still Going Strong for Private Tech
items.summary: Private tech investors continue to show strong enthusiasm for startups, contrasting with Wall Street's growing worries about overborrowing by AI-related companies and recent public market selloffs. This divergence was highlighted at Morgan Stanley's annual private tech conference in Dana Point, California, where investors eagerly engaged with startup founders, especially in defense and AI inference sectors. Morgan Stanley's head of technology equity, Diana Doyle, noted a clear disconnect between public and private market sentiments.

items.originalSummary:
The sentiment gap between public and private markets could not be wider right now. Wall Street investors have been increasingly worried about overborrowing by AI-related companies, as evidenced by skyrocketing yields on CoreWeave bonds, a selloff in semiconductor stocks and the yanking of the IPO of Firmus, the Australian data center operator.

Investors in private tech startups are still ebullient, blown away by how fast startups like Fireworks AI have grown. 

This bifurcation was evident to me this week at Morgan Stanley’s annual private tech companies conference. The mutual fund and other investors fanning out across a lush seaside resort in Dana Point, Calif., were aware of the red washing over trading screens. But that didn’t prevent them from rushing to meet the dozens of startup founders there, particularly if they were in the hot defense or inference sectors. 

“You can see there's a stark disconnect between the public markets and the private markets,” said Diana Doyle, Morgan Stanley’s head of technology equity and equity-linked capital markets on the sidelines of the conference.

items.originalTitle: Sega pulls Total War: Shogun 2 remaster from sale following disastrous launch
items.summary:
Sega has removed Total War: Shogun 2 — Complete Edition from digital storefronts following widespread user complaints about bugs and AI-upscaled graphics after its launch. The remaster, which includes the original game and all DLC with promised visual and control improvements, received overwhelmingly negative reviews on Steam and was quickly pulled from sale there.

Sega and developer Creative Assembly acknowledged the problems and said they are working with their development partner to fix the issues and restore quality. They plan to reinstate the original game while allowing existing owners continued access to the Complete Edition. The developer Mataboo is also involved in the project.

items.summary:
OpenAI has introduced the AI for Educators course in Brazilian Portuguese on its free OpenAI Academy platform, aimed at helping teachers in primary, secondary, and higher education use AI to plan lessons and create activities while maintaining pedagogical judgment. Alongside this, OpenAI launched Study Mode in ChatGPT, a tool designed to promote active, step-by-step learning by asking students questions, providing hints, and checking understanding.

Study Mode was developed with input from educators and experts to encourage reflection and reasoning, allowing students to engage deeply with subjects like biology or science through guided questioning. Teachers can also use the feature to assess student understanding and tailor classroom discussions. These tools were released on Teachers’ Day 2026 to highlight the evolving role of educators in integrating AI into learning environments.

items.title: Google launches Antigravity platform to accelerate discovery of novel antimicrobial peptides using AI-driven protein function prediction [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Accelerating the search for antimicrobial peptides with Google Antigravity
items.summary:
Google has introduced Antigravity, an agentic science workbench designed to speed up the search for new antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) by integrating multiple databases and leveraging AI models like ProtNLM to predict protein functions from amino acid sequences. This platform enables researchers to efficiently identify and structurally evaluate promising AMP candidates, compressing a traditionally fragmented process into a single interactive session.

Using Antigravity, biologists identified a novel antimicrobial peptide candidate from the Lactococcin 972 family with predicted activity against respiratory pathogens; this candidate is currently undergoing laboratory validation. The platform combines AI-driven sequence analysis, structural modeling via AlphaFold, and curated database searches to validate the novelty and potential efficacy of discovered peptides, addressing the urgent global challenge of rising antimicrobial resistance.

items.title: Trump posts AI-edited photo of White House column restoration on Truth Social, flagged by Google's AI detector [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Trump posts AI-edited photo to brag about White House restoration work
items.summary:
President Donald Trump shared a series of photos on Truth Social showcasing White House renovations, including one image of a column that appears to have been altered using AI. The AI-edited photo, which compares an old column to a "restored" one, shows inconsistencies such as mismatched steps and nearly identical angles, and was flagged by Google's SynthID Detector as created or edited with OpenAI technology.

Other photos posted by Trump showing the White House facade and heliport were not flagged, and real images from June show people painting the White House exterior, suggesting some restoration work did occur. The White House has not responded to requests for comment on the AI-edited image, while Trump has a history of posting AI-generated content.

items.title: Amazon devices chief Panos Panay envisions ambient AI devices replacing apps by anticipating user needs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Amazon devices chief Panos Panay sees a future where AI devices replace the need to use apps
items.summary:
Amazon's SVP of Devices, Panos Panay, outlined a vision for personal computing where ambient AI devices operate quietly in the background to anticipate and fulfill user needs, reducing reliance on traditional apps. He discussed this future during TechCrunch Disrupt alongside the launch of Amazon's new Bee AI wearables, which passively record and process audio to assist users while prioritizing privacy by not storing raw audio data.

Panay emphasized that this shift does not mean smartphones will disappear but that an intelligence layer connecting various devices will emerge to enhance user experience. He highlighted privacy as a critical design consideration for ambient computing, ensuring users maintain control over their data as AI devices become more integrated into daily life.

items.title: Anthropic grants METR researchers employee-level access to assess AI models and safety practices, allowing independent publication without company veto [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Anthropic is letting METR researchers look under the hood with employee-level access
items.summary:
Anthropic has given six researchers from the nonprofit METR employee-level access to its internal systems, including company laptops and office space, to independently evaluate its AI models, safety measures, and risk management. This move aims to increase transparency and accountability amid rising concerns about AI agents acting unpredictably. METR can publish its findings without Anthropic's approval, though certain sensitive information may be redacted under agreed terms.

The arrangement is part of a three-tier evaluation system Anthropic is developing, with METR at the top tier having the most comprehensive access. This initiative follows a broader industry trend toward independent oversight, with other major AI companies committing to similar review processes under a White House accord. Anthropic compares this setup to banking regulators embedding examiners within banks to monitor risks more effectively.

This expansion aims to enable everyday users, not just developers, to build social experiences connected to their Bluesky identities and audience.

Users can bring their own AI models or use open-weight options to create content that benefits from Bluesky's distribution network, which currently has 47 million registered users. The company plans to further support developers and communities with upcoming features like private data support, currently in alpha testing and expected to roll out by year-end.

items.originalTitle: Why AI-Written Software Needs a Flight Simulator
items.summary: As AI-generated applications become more common, companies are adopting deterministic simulators—software that repeatedly runs the same disaster scenarios—to identify and fix bugs caused by network issues or hacking attempts. Traditional stress-testing methods rely on developers anticipating problems, but these new simulators provide more reliable testing by simulating failures that humans might overlook, including attacks by rogue AIs. Replit's CTO Luis Chávez highlights the importance of these AI-assisted simulators in improving software resilience beyond what current AI code evaluation tools can achieve.

items.originalSummary:
As companies create more applications using AI, corporate officers say demand is rising for a new type of software that stress-tests those apps, simulating how they handle network problems and other disasters that humans may not think to test for—including cyberattacks by rogue AIs.

Luis Chávez, CTO of coding assistant provider Replit, says his company uses an AI-assisted software known as a deterministic simulator, a kind of flight simulator for software. The deterministic part refers to how the simulator lets companies run the same disaster test again and again so they can try out different fixes for bugs that crop up during network failures or hacking attempts.

Traditional stress-testing methods rely on developers guessing every potential problem that may arise. Merely using today’s AI models to evaluate code often produces false alarms or fake warnings, corporate executives say.

Researchers developed a voice agent based on large language models that can adhere to legally mandated conversational flows in debt collection calls, such as confirming the debtor's identity and avoiding prohibited language. They introduced FlowSpec, a machine-readable specification that generates policy instructions and supervises the agent's speech, enabling it to follow procedures it has never encountered before. The model was fine-tuned on 2,506 conversations from 297 randomized procedures and tested on four unseen deployment procedures, achieving significant improvements in compliance checks and scenario pass rates.

The study evaluated the agent on three debt collection and one non-debt procedure, including one from a completely withheld lineage, demonstrating that documented compliance checks rose from 67-71% to 93-100%, while grounded checks were already high before training. An audit of the shared specification revealed 11 defects, three of which were not detected by the agent's own metrics, highlighting areas for further refinement in regulatory adherence and testing.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.18881v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Voice agents built on large language models (LLMs) now handle customer calls, but in regulated applications completing the task is not enough: the agent must follow a conversational flow set by law. In debt collection, it must confirm it is speaking to the debtor before mentioning the debt, identify itself and the creditor, state the amount, and avoid prohibited language. Every creditor turns these rules into its own procedure and revises it. We ask whether a small, self-hosted policy can be trained once and then follow regulated procedures it has never seen. One machine-readable specification per deployment, FlowSpec, generates the policy instruction, gates the tools, supplies the supervision and defines the tests; the agent speaks only approved catalogue sentences. We fine-tune a 9-billion-parameter model on 2,506 conversations from 297 randomized procedures and evaluate a Thai outbound-call agent on four unseen deployment procedures (three debt collection, one non-debt), one from a wholly withheld lineage. Documented checks, fixed by the procedure, rise from 67--71 percents to 93--100 percents, while grounded checks, fixed by the conversation, already pass at 97--100 percents before training; scenario pass rate rises from 15/43 to 40/43. An audit of the shared specification finds 11 defects, 3 of which its own metric did not expose.

items.title: Researchers analyze how language models develop in-context learning, distinguishing copying from compositional understanding across 17 models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: From Copying to Composition: How Language Models Develop In-Context Learning
items.summary: Researchers studied in-context learning (ICL) in language models by separating copying behavior from integrating information across prompts, finding that about a third of 17 models prefer copied answers while others favor rule-consistent responses linked to higher accuracy. Their analysis showed models prioritize task-relevant prompt tokens before accuracy improves, and training with synthetic documents can shift models toward compositional responses. The study suggests ICL develops through distinct trajectories rather than as a single uniform capability, with aspects like prompt control and answer preference evolving separately.

The study suggests ICL develops through distinct trajectories rather than as a single uniform capability, with aspects like prompt control and answer preference evolving separately.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.19113v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In-context learning (ICL) allows language models to adapt their behavior from instructions and demonstrations in a prompt, but accuracy alone does not reveal how contextual information controls their predictions. We study the acquisition and trainability of ICL with a controlled diagnostic that separates copying a nearby demonstration from integrating information across the prompt. Across 17 models, about a third prefer the copied answer, a few are undecided, and the rest prefer the rule-consistent answer, which goes with higher accuracy and with control by the requested value rather than the closest conflicting example. Checkpoint analyses show that models begin prioritizing task-relevant prompt tokens over conflicting examples long before their accuracy improves beyond chance level. In matched training experiments, synthetic documents that define endings and then query them shift models toward compositional responses on the controlled diagnostic, whereas fine-tuning on definition exercises built from rewritten real documents improves accuracy when prompts reassign label meanings. The results suggest that ICL is not acquired as a single, uniform capability. Instead, prompt control, answer preference, construction without candidates, and transfer can develop along distinct trajectories.

items.title: Researchers analyze Best-of-N sampling in large language models as a competition between reward tails of correct and incorrect responses, identifying regimes that explain scaling and degradation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Tail Competition Explains Scaling in Best-of-N Sampling for Verifiable Problems
items.summary:
Researchers study Best-of-N sampling, a strategy for scaling large language models at inference time, by modeling it as a competition between the extreme reward tails of correct and incorrect outputs. They identify three asymptotic regimes—correct-tail-dominant, incorrect-tail-dominant, and critical—that explain both performance gains and reward-hacking-induced degradation. Using extreme value theory, they derive finite-sample scaling laws and show that incorrect responses with high variance can dominate selection even if their mean reward is lower, leading to polynomial rather than exponential convergence with incomplete selectors.

The study proposes a tail-tension criterion to predict when additional sampling may harm performance. Experiments on synthetic data and real reward model scores align with the theoretical predictions, suggesting that tail competition offers a unified framework for understanding Best-of-N sampling behavior in verifiable problems.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.19362v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Best-of-N sampling is a simple inference-time scaling strategy for large language models, yet its behavior under incomplete reward models remains poorly understood. We study Best-of-N as a competition between the extreme reward tails of correct and incorrect responses. This view shows that success depends not only on the probability of sampling a correct response, but also on whether correct responses dominate incorrect ones in the upper tail. Using extreme value theory, we characterize three asymptotic regimes: correct-tail-dominant, incorrect-tail-dominant, and critical explaining both monotonic gains and reward-hacking-induced degradation. We further derive finite-sample scaling laws for representative reward distributions, showing that, under Gaussian rewards, incorrect responses with sufficiently large variance can dominate selection even when their mean reward is lower. Unlike oracle selection, convergence with an incomplete selector can be polynomial rather than exponential. Finally, we propose a lightweight tail-tension criterion to estimate when additional sampling may become harmful. Experiments on synthetic data and real reward model scores are consistent with the theoretically predicted regimes, scaling laws, and diagnostic behavior, suggesting that tail competition provides a unified lens on Best-of-N sampling for verifiable problems.

items.title: Researchers compare typed decision models and large language models on tabular data tasks, finding decision models match LLM performance at lower cost but lack robustness to table organization [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Typed Decision Models on Tabular Data
items.summary: Researchers studied typed decision models, which output probabilities for fixed answer sets, on tabular data tasks including row classification, fact verification, and anomaly detection. They compared four decision models with three large language models (LLMs) using original and 21 rewritten versions of queries that preserved content but altered format or wording. The decision models performed as well as LLMs at a lower computational cost and showed greater robustness to question formulation, but none of the models were robust to changes in table organization, with at least a third of row decisions changing under some rewrites. Decisions with low probability were most likely to vary. The study highlights decision models as practical for tabular data tasks while emphasizing the ongoing challenge of improving their robustness.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.19536v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Typed decision models are language models that answer a question with a fixed set of possible answers by returning a probability for each answer instead of generating text. We study them on tabular data and compare four decision models with three large language models (LLMs) on row classification, fact verification and anomaly detection. Every request is sent in its original form and under 21 types of rewrite that keep its content, such as renaming the options or writing the table in another format. The decision models perform as well as the LLMs at a lower cost. Three of them are also far more robust to how the question is formulated. No model we test is robust to how the table is organized. For every model, at least a third of the row decisions change under some rewrite of the table or the question. The decisions to which a decision model gives low probability are the ones most likely to change. Decision models are a practical choice for tabular decisions, but their robustness remains an open problem.

items.title: Researchers develop automated model to predict suspected overdose deaths from investigation reports, outperforming current rule-based systems by 15% [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Evidence-Anchored Overdose Death Prediction from Death Investigation Reports
items.summary:
Researchers have created an automated framework that classifies suspected overdose deaths using death investigation reports, which are often underutilized due to delays in certifying drug-involved deaths in the US. The model generates expert-guided explanations and improves prediction accuracy compared to existing rule-based systems.

The study compares pipeline models that first rationalize then predict with self-rationalizing models that do both simultaneously, finding that pipeline models with explanations grounded in the reports perform best. The approach also allows expert intervention for final decisions, enhancing practical applicability in death investigations.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.19556v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Confirmation of overdose deaths in the United States is often delayed due to the complexities of certifying drug-involved deaths. Death investigation reports represent a rich but underutilized data source that could be used to predict whether a death is a suspected overdose (i.e., a death preliminarily identified as an overdose prior to the final cause and manner of death determination). We present an automated framework that classifies suspected overdoses from death investigation reports, while producing supporting explanations guided by expert knowledge. Through an expert-guided design process, we investigate 1) what type of explanations are best for model prediction performance, and 2) which architecture is better suited for this task: pipeline models that rationalize first and then predict, or self-rationalizing models that jointly predict and rationalize? Our experiments show that a pipeline model with explanations grounded in the input death investigation reports outperforms the other settings. Our best model also outperforms a rule-based system currently in deployment by 15%, while allowing expert interventions for final decisions.

items.title: DAGFormer introduces a jointly trained topology predictor for Transformer cross-layer connections, improving perplexity and accuracy across multiple tasks compared to vanilla models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: DAGFormer: Global Topology Prediction for Transformer Cross-Layer Connections
items.summary:
DAGFormer is a Transformer language model that uses a jointly trained topology predictor to plan cross-layer connections globally, adding direct links from earlier to later layers controlled by input tokens. This approach differs from existing architectures that set connections separately for each layer. DAGFormer achieves 17% to 25% lower perplexity on WikiText-2 compared to standard Transformers and outperforms baseline routing models across parameter scales from 75 million to 1 billion.

The model's improvements extend to 13 evaluation tasks in commonsense, science, reading, and math, showing 2.0 to 2.5 points higher mean accuracy at 300 million and 1 billion parameters. It also leads in instruction finetuning with a 63% to 70% win rate against vanilla Transformers on AlpacaEval. Under structured pruning, DAGFormer maintains performance better than baselines in most settings, demonstrating robustness and efficiency gains.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.19625v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose DAGFormer, a Transformer language model whose cross-layer connections are planned by a jointly trained topology predictor. Beyond the residual connections in a standard Transformer, DAGFormer adds direct connections from earlier layers to later ones, and the predictor controls the strength of every connection based on input tokens. Unlike existing cross-layer routing architectures, which set each layer's connections separately, DAGFormer plans the routing of the whole model at once. On matched OLMo-2 pairs from 75M to 1B parameters, DAGFormer lowers WikiText-2 perplexity by 17% to 25% over the vanilla Transformer, and a 1B DAGFormer trained on 5B tokens outperforms the vanilla model trained on 10B. Against four routing baselines with the same data and budget, it reaches the lowest perplexity at 75M, 300M and 1B. The gain carries over to 13 commonsense, science, reading and math evaluation tasks (2.0 to 2.5 points higher mean accuracy at 300M and 1B) and to instruction finetuning (63% to 70% AlpacaEval win rate against the vanilla Transformer, leading every routing baseline), and under structured pruning DAGFormer degrades the least in five of six settings.

items.title: HACHIMI-II models learner behavior to improve student simulation accuracy, reducing ability prediction errors by up to 8.4 times and better reproducing real student errors [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: HACHIMI-II: From Role-Play to Learner Behavior Modeling for Faithful Student Simulation
items.summary:
HACHIMI-II introduces a student simulation approach that predicts a learner's next action based on their history and current state, rather than relying on large language models to role-play students. This method improves the fidelity of simulated students by more accurately reflecting where individual learners succeed and fail, making it useful for testing tutoring systems before real learners are available.

The system was evaluated on three item-response datasets and two dialogue datasets, showing significant improvements over previous baselines in matching real student abilities and error patterns. These gains are attributed mainly to the explicit modeling of the learner's state, enabling more realistic and varied student simulations.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.19654v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Simulated students let researchers test tutoring systems and teaching strategies before real learners are available, but only if the simulation reproduces where a particular learner succeeds and fails. The common approach asks a large language model to role-play a student, but a role does not model what this learner knows or will do next, so the model's own competence fills the gap. Simulated students perform at a level set by the model, differ little from one another, and seldom make the real learners' errors. We model the learner's behavior and recast student simulation as third-person prediction of the learner's next action. HACHIMI-II builds a student model from the learner's history, infers the learner's state for the current item or tutor turn, and compiles it into a behavior harness that constrains the next action. On three item-response datasets, the Wasserstein-1 distance between simulated and real student ability is 2.4--8.4$\times$ smaller than that of the strongest baseline. On two dialogue datasets, HACHIMI-II reproduces real student errors with the same knowledge type, locus, and mechanism 1.8--5.1$\times$ more often than the strongest baseline, and ablations trace the gains mainly to the explicit learner state. Predicting the learner makes capable models usable as simulated students.

items.title: Researchers introduce AtomSearch, a tree search method for optimizing agent skills through local rule edits and skill-state evaluation, outperforming SkillOpt on multiple tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: AtomSearch: Evidence-Grounded Tree Search for Agent Skill Optimization
items.summary: AtomSearch is a new approach for adapting agent skills by applying local edits to frozen models and using subsequent skill states to guide search. It links each rule edit to execution outcomes and uses a Skill-State Tree Search to evaluate and retain promising edit sequences. The method was tested on four tasks and five models, showing improvements over SkillOpt, including a 9.68-percentage-point gain on LiveMathematicianBench and more compact skill representations. The results demonstrate that local rule edits can effectively explore useful revision paths and produce efficient skills, with additional offline evaluations exploring alternative states.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.19951v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agent skills adapt frozen models through editable external instructions. Revising several rules at once makes changes difficult to inspect, while judging each local edit only by its immediate score can discard useful intermediate states. We introduce AtomSearch, which keeps revision actions local while using subsequent skill states to guide search. Contrastive atomic editing links each primitive rule edit to failed and successful executions, a behavioral hypothesis, and an intended scope. Skill-State Tree Search (STS) evaluates short edit compositions and selectively retains them as executable states that can be revisited and extended. Outcome memory supplies later proposals with observed repair and regression statistics. We evaluate AtomSearch across four tasks and five target models. With deepseek-v4-flash, it exceeds SkillOpt on three of four tasks, including a 9.68-percentage-point gain on LiveMathematicianBench, and SkillOpt's final skills contain 2.3-19.7 times as many characters. In 67% of completed searches, the best validation state passes through an ancestor that was not highest-scoring at its depth. These results show how local rule edits can support the exploration of useful revision paths and yield compact skills, with additional offline evaluations used to explore alternative states.

items.title: Researchers test cross-model in-context neurofeedback to assess activation control in large language models, finding limited ability in some models to modulate their own activations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Cross-Model In-Context Neurofeedback Reveals (Limited) Activation Control in LLMs
items.summary:
Researchers conducted experiments using in-context neurofeedback sessions to determine whether large language models (LLMs) can control their own activation vectors, which are often used to detect misbehavior. They tested ten open-weight models ranging from 9 billion to 32 billion parameters, asking models to maximize or minimize scores derived from their activations while generating or responding to sentences. Some models showed the ability to influence their activation scores, but this effect was comparable to that of a separate writer model, suggesting limited genuine control.

Further tests involved fixing the model's responses and asking it to adjust activation scores, revealing that three out of ten models exhibited small but consistent control effects. The study also explored whether models could manipulate activations to evade detection by activation monitors, such as deception detectors; no model successfully lowered flagged scores, though one could raise them. The findings indicate that while some LLMs have limited in-context control over their activations, this capability is not yet sufficient to undermine activation monitoring but warrants ongoing observation as models evolve.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.20179v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Probes on activation vectors are widely used to detect misbehavior in language models, but their success relies on the assumption that models cannot control what their activations encode. Humans can learn, through neurofeedback, to control the firing of even single neurons, and recent studies investigated whether this ability extends to language models, reaching conflicting conclusions. No experimental design so far disentangles competence at the task from genuine access to one's own activations. We fill this gap with in-context neurofeedback sessions, in which a "subject" model is asked to maximize (or minimize) a score derived from its activations, shown back to it at every turn. In our first experiment, the sentences are generated either by the subject or by a second "writer" model, while the score always derives from the activations of the subject. We test ten open-weight models from five families, with sizes from 9B to 32B. Some models move their own scores considerably, but no more than a writer of comparable competence moves them. Is this because the task requires no privileged access, or because the subject controls its activations while processing the sentences, whoever wrote them? To answer this, we prefill a fixed sentence as the subject's reply at every turn and ask it to increase or decrease the score. Three out of ten models show small but consistent control effects. We further ask whether models can control their activations to the point of fooling an activation monitor. We make models repeat sentences a monitor would flag, such as a deceptive answer for a deception monitor, and ask them to raise or lower the monitor's score. No model learns to lower it, but one model can raise it. In-context control of a model's own activations might not yet be a threat to activation monitors, but it exists in a few models and needs to be tracked as models evolve.

items.title: Researchers propose Cortex to consolidate context gains into parametric memory for large language models, improving retention across 4B–120B parameter models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Cortex: Consolidating Context into Parametric Memory
items.summary: Researchers introduce Cortex, a method inspired by biological memory consolidation, to internalize context-induced performance gains in large language models while preserving unrelated capabilities. Cortex anticipates future context use through prospective queries and distills context-conditioned outputs into mergeable low-rank or structural feed-forward network updates. The approach was evaluated across multiple model sizes and architectures, including text-only and multimodal models, demonstrating strong consolidation and retention performance. After 50 sequential factual edits on a 14B parameter model, Cortex-Structural recovered 88.9% of context gains while maintaining 99.8% of original non-target performance, indicating effective memory consolidation without significant degradation of existing skills.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.20399v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Context can improve large language model performance, but these gains may be lost after context removal. Inspired by biological systems consolidation, we formulate Memory Consolidation (MC) as internalizing these gains while preserving non-target capabilities, connecting context-specified editing, skill learning, and behavioral steering under a common objective. We introduce a five-task-family testbed measuring consolidation and retention under single, batch, and sequential updates. We propose Cortex, which generates prospective queries to anticipate uses of context and distills context-conditioned outputs into mergeable low-rank or structural feed-forward network updates. Across 4B--120B dense and mixture-of-experts backbones, including both text-only and multimodal models, Cortex lies on the empirical consolidation--retention Pareto frontier in most evaluated settings. After 50 sequential factual edits on a 14B model, Cortex-Structural recovers 88.9% of the context-induced gain while retaining 99.8% of original non-target performance.

items.title: VASPO: Self-Distillation with Privileged Value Estimation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: VASPO: Self-Distillation with Privileged Value Estimation
items.summary: arXiv:2610.20516v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: On-policy self-distillation provides dense supervision for reasoning models via a privileged self-teacher. However, this supervision reflects local token preferences rather than the expected return of an unguided student continuation. Recent methods combine this signal with GRPO. They use GRPO for update directions and the teacher for signal scaling. However, we demonstrate a more effective integration within PPO. Specifically, we identify complementary positional dynamics: privileged information enhances a critic's value-prediction accuracy toward the response's end, whereas self-teacher guidance is strong initially, drops mid-generation, and rebounds finally. These insights motivate Value-Augmented Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (VASPO), wherein a self-teacher and critic evaluate identical privileged information at student-generated prefixes. The critic computes token-level PPO advantages from predicted continuation returns, while the self-teacher modulates selected positive advantages via bounded probability ratios. Across six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, VASPO improves mean accuracy over PPO by 2.59 and 1.81 percentage points on Qwen3-4B and OLMo3-7B variants, respectively, and achieves the highest mean accuracy among evaluated methods on Knights and Knaves. Our code is available at https://github.com/cii030/VASPO.

items.title: PrismaCoder: Pushing the Boundaries of Open Multimodal Code Intelligence through Decomposed Rubric Synthesis [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: PrismaCoder: Pushing the Boundaries of Open Multimodal Code Intelligence through Decomposed Rubric Synthesis
items.summary: arXiv:2610.20538v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal code intelligence connects the symbolic world of programs with the visual world their execution creates. Interest in this capability is burgeoning, as models are increasingly asked to produce charts, webpages, animations, and semi-structured documents. Recently, proprietary models have pushed far ahead, producing interactive artifacts even from a text description or a screenshot alone. Yet their data and training remain closed, and open progress is held back by the quantity and quality of available data and by the pipelines and methods for producing it. Quality is the harder of the two, since a sample must be correct as a program, well built, and above all visually right once rendered. No existing signal covers all three. Execution often returns just a pass or fail, code similarity does not map to the visual output, and task-specific verifiers do not generalize. To push open progress further, we start from the data side with PrismaForge, a hierarchical data pipeline centered on a synthesized rubric that decomposes these factors into checkable criteria. The same rubric serves as both filter and reward: it curates the supervised corpus, then drives reinforcement learning on visual-coding tasks. Leveraging PrismaForge for data synthesis and filtering, we build PrismaCoder-2M, the most diverse open dataset for multimodal code intelligence and the largest to date. On the model side, we train PrismaCoder-9B and PrismaCoder-35B on this data and release both. They lead the open state of the art by a wide margin and rival leading proprietary systems. Our analyses further show that the proposed rubric-based pipeline improves multimodal coding performance across model backbones. We release our code and data at https://qiushisun.github.io/PrismaCoder-Home/.

items.title: Lotus: Learning to Understand Time-series by Learning to Forecast [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Lotus: Learning to Understand Time-series by Learning to Forecast
items.summary: arXiv:2610.18877v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Time-series language models typically align numerical signals with language using labels, captions, or question-answer pairs. Although such supervision encourages linguistic representations, it does not explicitly require them to preserve information about how the underlying time-series signal evolves. We introduce forecast grounding, a pretraining principle that requires language-aligned time-series representations to remain predictive of the future evolution before they are adapted to downstream tasks. We instantiate this principle in LOTUS, which divides each time-series channel into non-overlapping patches and maps them into the LLM embedding space. It then predicts the next patch from the LLM hidden states of the time-series tokens, encouraging the learned representation to retain temporal information. To capture both temporal changes and periodic patterns, we also propose a temporal-spectral patch representation that combines each raw time-series patch with its spectral representation before mapping it into the LLM embedding space. Across three language model backbones and six downstream evaluation datasets, LOTUS achieves the best average performance with minimal trainable parameters, reaching 59.91% accuracy and outperforming the strongest matched baseline by 3.36%. Our representation analyses further show that LOTUS uses the numerical input and preserves temporal structure in its learned patch representations. These results establish forecast grounding as a promising pretraining principle, enabling compact time-series language models to outperform models 25 to 50 times their size on TSRBench.

items.title: The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery
items.summary: arXiv:2610.18933v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern coding agents are fundamentally reshaping the role of human input for computational research: they write code, launch in silico experiments, analyze their results, and autonomously operate with ever-increasing time horizons. Despite these developments, fully autonomous research agents suffer from a limited ideation radius and myopic hill-climbing search dynamics. To bridge this gap, we introduce The Agentic Scientist, an end-to-end distributed pipeline for human researchers to conduct computational research alongside modern coding agents. Building on its predecessor, our system decomposes research into task drafting, idea generation, planning, sandboxed experimentation, result aggregation, baseline and ablation construction, post-hoc analysis, and report writing. Importantly, each step in the pipeline is powered by the next generation of coding agents and leverages agentic self-verification. The overall research process is driven by a meta-controller that manages parallel research agents and enforces rubric verification at each stage. This design enables the same orchestration layer to be reused across heterogeneous domains with different execution environments, agentic coding harnesses, and evaluation metrics. Our system can be used across a spectrum of autonomy: either as a co-scientist tool or to perform end-to-end scientific investigation. Within the co-scientist setting, we leveraged a development version of our system to submit a single research paper, which got accepted for publication at ALIFE 2026. We further apply The Agentic Scientist fully autonomously to open problem-solving tasks in machine learning, and demonstrate the system's capability of scientific discovery across different domains of computational research. Our ablations suggest that reliable scientific autonomy depends not only on base model capabilities, but also on the cross-agent orchestration layer.

items.title: Who Should We Listen to More? Welfare-Aware Preference Acquisition for Pluralistic Alignment [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Who Should We Listen to More? Welfare-Aware Preference Acquisition for Pluralistic Alignment
items.summary: arXiv:2610.19035v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pluralistic alignment needs to accommodate diverse preferences under limited human feedback. Using AI simulators to label preference comparisons reduces annotation costs, but variation in simulation accuracy across individuals can leave some people's preferences poorly represented in training. We study how to allocate human feedback across people to construct training data for pluralistic alignment, and how this allocation affects the trained policy. To make this allocation explicit and controllable, we define a social welfare objective over individual supervision utilities that measure label quality. Each query's marginal welfare gain depends on its expected supervision improvement, the recipient's current utility, and application-designated priority. Welfare-Aware Preference Acquisition (WAPA) uses auxiliary reference models to estimate query gains and individual utilities, then selects queries by estimated marginal welfare gain while updating recipient utilities. We prove exact optimality of the acquisition algorithm for the estimated welfare objective under a fixed query budget and model predictions. Experiments on six Roleplay collections and four OpinionQA regions demonstrate improved supervision and controllable allocation tradeoffs. Policy training on four Roleplay collections improves preference prediction for both seen and unseen individuals. When prioritizing a designated group and poorly represented individuals, acquiring human labels for 20% of comparisons recovers 75-86% of the average predictive utility gap between policies trained entirely on AI-generated labels and entirely on ground-truth labels.

items.title: Graph Coarsening Enables Escaping Local Optima in Compute-Constrained Nonconvex MAX-CUT [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Graph Coarsening Enables Escaping Local Optima in Compute-Constrained Nonconvex MAX-CUT
items.summary: arXiv:2610.19043v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Because its binary optimization landscape contains exponentially many local optima, MAX-CUT is highly sensitive to initialization. We study Particle Polynomial Relaxation (PPR), a moment-based nonconvex continuous reformulation possessing an advantageous optimization landscape. We warm-start PPR with Combinatorial Multigrid (CMG), a spectral graph-coarsening method that produces structure-aware initial solutions in near-linear time without training data. On \texttt{t2g20} ($n=400$), benchmark instance with known exact optimum, the combined CMG+PPR pipeline reaches $97.5\%$ of optimum on average and $98.4\%$ on the best run. An extended variant with discrete local-search refinement reaches the published optimum on all sixty Biq Mac instances evaluated by a recent neural branch-and-bound method. Using a sparse CSR representation, the same approach scales to G-set instances with up to $20{,}000$ vertices reducing memory requirements by up to $3333\times$ while maintaining a consistent improvement over the CMG warm start. Gains are largest on sparse weighted graphs; on dense graphs we complement the pipeline with spectral sparsification.

items.title: Smart Alone, Blind Together: Why Accuracy Fails to CertifyTheory of Mind in Multi-Agent Teams [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Smart Alone, Blind Together: Why Accuracy Fails to CertifyTheory of Mind in Multi-Agent Teams
items.summary: arXiv:2610.19051v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coordinators that act on what they infer about teammates are usually certified by the accuracy of those inferences. We argue that accuracy is the wrong certificate, for two reasons. First, the accuracy needed to act depends on what a wrong action costs, so the bar belongs to the deployment, not the module. Second, a module's errors are rarely independent, and dependence has a sign: positively associated errors help where their damage overlaps and hurt where it compounds, so an accuracy threshold fails in a predictable direction, and once wrong beliefs interact and can do harm, no rule based on accuracy is right for every module. We test these predictions in task assignment, Level-Based Foraging and Hanabi, with injected errors, trained and Bayesian modules and five language models, and in human judgments. Accuracy fails in both directions, approving harmful language-model deployments in Hanabi, where shared errors compound, and rejecting beneficial ones in task assignment, where costly errors are rare. In our tasks it also buys far less redundancy than independence predicts: from GPT-5.4-mini to Claude Opus 5.5, error on teammates the models have evidence about falls from 32% to 11%, but the chance that all three observers misread one falls only from 16% to 9% (independence: 3.4% to 0.15%). We propose certifying the deployment, with a Blind-Spot Gate that prices error costs, pairwise interactions and measured dependence without deploying the module. On held-out data from the cells it was developed on, it makes no significant false approval in 20 splits (accuracy: 3.2 per split), and in preregistered tests on modules it was not developed on, it recovers what accuracy rejects (seven classifiers: regret 0.004 against 0.479) and catches what accuracy approves (a Bayesian module: significant false approvals in 17 of 20 splits for accuracy, 1 for the gate).

We propose certifying the deployment, with a Blind-Spot Gate that prices error costs, pairwise interactions and measured dependence without deploying the module. On held-out data from the cells it was developed on, it makes no significant false approval in 20 splits (accuracy: 3.2 per split), and in preregistered tests on modules it was not developed on, it recovers what accuracy rejects (seven classifiers: regret 0.004 against 0.479) and catches what accuracy approves (a Bayesian module: significant false approvals in 17 of 20 splits for accuracy, 1 for the gate).

items.title: Beyond Aggregate Accuracy: Item-Level Transitions in Prompt Optimization [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Beyond Aggregate Accuracy: Item-Level Transitions in Prompt Optimization
items.summary: arXiv:2610.19084v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Automatic prompt optimization (APO) uses feedback from model responses to improve prompts automatically. However, its effectiveness is usually measured through overall scores, which do not reveal which questions become correct, which previously correct answers become wrong, or whether improvements extend to unseen questions. We introduce Reflective Feedback-Driven Prompt Optimization (RFDPO), a tool that tracks recoveries (incorrect to correct), regressions (correct to incorrect), and churn (all changed outcomes). RFDPO uses this feedback to guide subsequent revisions and records prompt changes throughout optimization. We evaluate RFDPO across five benchmarks covering law, knowledge, instruction following, mathematics, and privacy, using GPT-5 as the optimizer and GPT-4o-mini and GPT-4.1 Mini as solvers. Our results show that overall accuracy can hide substantial changes: in five of nine configurations, churn was at least five times the absolute net change, and a single-item net change concealed up to 17 changed outcomes. Average validation gains were 7.9 percentage points, compared with 5.2 points on held-out tests. In a controlled ablation on LegalBench-Hearsay, item-level feedback reduced churn by 40% ($p=0.024$) while maintaining similar net gains. These findings motivate reporting recovery, regression, churn, and performance on unseen data alongside overall accuracy.

items.title: Unlocking Structured Pruning for Reasoning Language Models via Attention-Preserving MLP Trimming [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Unlocking Structured Pruning for Reasoning Language Models via Attention-Preserving MLP Trimming
items.summary: arXiv:2610.19121v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Structured pruning reduces LLM inference costs by removing model components to produce smaller dense models. However, existing methods can cause reasoning performance to collapse on long-form reasoning tasks such as AIME. We propose \textit{LayerTrim}, a training-free structured pruning method that identifies redundant decoder layers and selectively trims their MLP features while preserving attention and decoder depth. LayerTrim is the first training-free structured pruning method designed to preserve long-form reasoning without gradients or recovery training. Across three reasoning language models and five benchmarks, LayerTrim outperforms existing structured pruning methods in most evaluated settings, improving average accuracy by up to 21.4 percentage points over RESP. On \texttt{Qwen3-14B}, LayerTrim achieves 1.24$\times$ faster prefill and 19.7\% lower peak GPU memory than the dense model, while better preserving reasoning ability. It also achieves the shortest average generation length among evaluated pruned models, while retaining the highest average accuracy. These results demonstrate that LayerTrim improves reasoning efficiency through both structural compression and reduced token generation.

items.title: MA-Bench: Measuring Operational Planning in Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: MA-Bench: Measuring Operational Planning in Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2610.19138v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How well can a language model turn a large, incomplete and partly contradictory body of documents into a plan when no single correct answer exists? We introduce Mission Analysis (MA)-Bench, built on mission analysis, the first step of military operational planning, in which a staff reads the full situation and states the problem before anyone proposes a solution. Its 10 expert-built scenarios pair synthetic packets of ten to twelve documents with 1,257 expert-written pass/fail requirements, each containing information on their source, question type, and importance level. A reasoning-model judge grades each brief against the requirements without seeing the documents; it grades like a fifth credentialed planner, leaving a four-planner panel's agreement unchanged (Fleiss $\kappa$ 0.42 to 0.41), and a judge from a second provider reproduces the model ranking (Spearman 0.94). Across twenty frontier and open-weights models the best gets 62% of the rubric items right. Models are strongest on facts stated in the documents (58%) and weakest on judgments that must be inferred (33%), and six failures in ten are omissions rather than errors. MA-Bench grades the determinations, not the prose. We release the packets, rubrics, prompts, scorer and every graded brief with item-level verdicts.

items.title: Into the Unknown: Benchmarking AI agents on open scientific research problems [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Into the Unknown: Benchmarking AI agents on open scientific research problems
items.summary: arXiv:2610.19159v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Can AI agents carry out research on open scientific problems? We introduce Into the Unknown, a benchmark that provides an agent with a science paper along with a research direction to pursue and tasks it to write a follow-up paper. We work with scientists at US Department of Energy (DOE) national laboratories, who each contribute an unpublished follow-up direction from their own work together with the necessary conditions a submission must meet. While assessing the quality of a follow-up paper is challenging in general, using these conditions to form a rubric makes evaluation more tractable for research problems that have no reference answer. We have nine frontier agents write 15 follow-ups each, spanning quantum computing, plasma physics, computational chemistry, materials science, and scientific machine learning domains. None of the 135 submissions satisfies all the conditions, and 114 fail our integrity check, most often because the paper claims work that was never done or reports numbers that contradict the recorded evidence. Overall, agents readily produce papers that look like follow-ups, but none meets the standard of the domain scientist, leaving substantial headroom. Our code and data are publicly available.

items.title: Steering Vectors for Competing Ethical Frameworks Are Interchangeable: A Competing-Target Test for Activation Steering [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Steering Vectors for Competing Ethical Frameworks Are Interchangeable: A Competing-Target Test for Activation Steering
items.summary: arXiv:2610.19359v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Activation steering adds a vector to a model's hidden states to control a named behaviour. A gain on that behaviour, however, does not show that the vector controls it directly: it may act through a component shared with neighbouring behaviours, which unsteered and random baselines cannot separate. We introduce the competing-target test: a vector is compared with the vector built the same way for a competing target, and an equivalence test states when their difference is below a useful margin. We apply it in open-weight models to vectors for Kantian deontology, which judges an act by the rule it follows, and act utilitarianism, which judges it by the welfare it produces. On held-out situations, prompting a framework raises its score and lowers the other's, whereas vectors for either framework move both scores alike, and none reaches the margin. The two vectors share most of their direction, a request to apply some framework; the same construction separates an optimistic from a pessimistic tone, whose vectors share much less. What a vector shares with its competitors therefore sets what it controls: steering a perspective can deliver a mixture, and measuring a disposition can measure its neighbours, unless tested against the competing target.

items.title: Who's Behind the Text? Robust Model Authorship Attribution [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Who's Behind the Text? Robust Model Authorship Attribution
items.summary: arXiv:2610.19583v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate text, their misuse has become a growing societal problem, with implications for academic misconduct, model distillation, and cyberattacks. For these reasons, Model Authorship Attribution (MAA), which identifies the source model of a given text, is important for promoting the responsible use of LLMs and improving AI safety. In practice, attribution systems must remain reliable beyond the distributions observed during training. They may encounter texts from unseen domains and writing settings, as well as generations from future versions of model families that were not available when the system was trained. However, existing MAA methods often exhibit substantial performance degradation under such distribution shifts. To address this challenge, we propose Authorship Tracing via Likelihood-based Attribution of Sources (ATLAS), which formulates MAA through source-conditioned text modeling rather than direct source prediction. ATLAS learns how text from each source family is generated and attributes a given text by comparing its likelihood under each learned source condition. We aggregate this likelihood evidence at the token level with clipping so that no single token dominates the decision. We further introduce MAABench, a broad MAA benchmark for evaluating practical OOD settings such as domain and version. Our experiments show that ATLAS consistently outperforms existing baselines across MAABench and OpenTuringBench. In particular, when both the generation domain and the model version change on MAABench, ATLAS achieves 74.27% accuracy, 9.00pp higher than the strongest baseline. Beyond MAA, ATLAS can also help identify distillation source models by measuring which source model a target LLM most closely resembles. Our extended experiments show that ATLAS recovers the known teacher of every distilled model we evaluate.
items.description: arXiv:2610.19583v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate text, their misuse has become a growing societal problem, with implications for academic misconduct, model distillation, and cyberattacks. In practice, attribution systems must remain reliable beyond the distributions observed during training. Our experiments show that ATLAS consistently outperforms existing baselines across MAABench and OpenTuringBench. In particular, when both the generation domain and the model version change on MAABench, ATLAS achieves 74.27% accuracy, 9.00pp higher than the strongest baseline. Beyond MAA, ATLAS can also help identify distillation source models by measuring which source model a target LLM most closely resembles. Our extended experiments show that ATLAS recovers the known teacher of every distilled model we evaluate.

items.title: Divergent Paths: Learning an Outcome-Predictive Representation of LLM Agent Trajectories [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Divergent Paths: Learning an Outcome-Predictive Representation of LLM Agent Trajectories
items.summary: arXiv:2610.19614v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this work, we reframe agentic trajectories as paths through a shared embedding space of actions and environmental observations. We show that successful and failed rollouts of the same task separate in this space, with simple per-task discriminators predicting held-out rollout outcomes at up to 0.95 AUROC across three agent benchmarks and three policy models. To exploit this signal across tasks, we introduce Precog-RM, a transformer-based model that meta-learns a representation in which outcome prediction can be performed in a few-shot setting. We show that Precog-RM generalizes to unseen tasks and models, and gives confident predictions of trajectory success long before termination. Deployed as an early stopping controller for Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on Tau2-Bench, Precog-RM cuts training FLOPs by up to 47.3\% while maintaining performance comparable to baseline GRPO.

items.title: Sparse Autoencoders Are a Shared Coordinate System for Symbolic Matching [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Sparse Autoencoders Are a Shared Coordinate System for Symbolic Matching
items.summary: arXiv:2610.19636v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) hold broad knowledge in one set of weights, but lack interpretability and trustworthy reasoning, especially in high-stakes use cases. A neuro-symbolic model, with its interpretable architecture and System 2 reasoning capacity, is a promising alternative if built at the scale of LLMs; however, its symbolic backbone is usually constructed with human effort, so existing neuro-symbolic models are bottlenecked by the scope of the symbol component and usually domain-specific. A data-driven method could instead build a larger symbolic system by aligning and merging existing ones. We target its first, foundational step: matching units across these heterogeneous systems. Our method, SAE-IDF, encodes a symbol in its native context into a sparse code with a sparse autoencoder (SAE), re-weights each dimension by its rarity and matches across systems. On 12 tasks across 6 kinds of symbolic system, SAE-IDF outperforms the same LLM's dense baseline on all tasks with Gemma-2-9B and all but one with Llama-3.1-8B, by up to 45 points, consistently across SAE layers and configurations. SAE-IDF is also interpretable: every dimension of the sparse code has a human-readable meaning, so each match decomposes into named concepts (features). Our work paves the way to a universal symbolic backbone.

items.title: Model What Matters: Decision-Guided Selective World Modeling for Language Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Model What Matters: Decision-Guided Selective World Modeling for Language Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2610.19642v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning provides a direct mechanism for optimizing task objectives in large language model-driven agents, but task rewards are typically sparse trajectory-level signals that only evaluate task success, without directly supervising action-conditioned environment transitions, leaving the model with limited explicit understanding of action consequences and environment dynamics. Recent work introduces auxiliary supervision through policy and world modeling co-training, yet typically treats complete environmental observations uniformly as world modeling targets, overlooking the varying decision relevance of observation content. We propose DGS-WM (Decision-Guided Selective World Modeling), a decision-guided policy-world modeling co-training approach for language agents. DGS-WM employs a Decision-Guided Observation Selection component that filters observation units with decision value as world modeling targets based on their support for subsequent policy responses, and a Confidence-Adaptive Weighting component that adaptively adjusts supervision strength according to the model's prediction confidence on selected targets. Together, these components form a decision-aware auxiliary world modeling loss, jointly optimized with the RL loss on the same policy model. Across multiple benchmarks covering single-hop/multi-hop question answering and interactive web tasks, DGS-WM achieves consistent improvements under different model scales and RL algorithms, demonstrating more stable and effective performance compared to full-observation world modeling methods.

items.title: Function-Space Temporal Self-Distillation for Policy Optimization [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Function-Space Temporal Self-Distillation for Policy Optimization
items.summary: arXiv:2610.19687v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) improves reasoning in language models, but scalar outcomes provide coarse supervision over response trajectories. Self-distillation offers denser token-level guidance by comparing an unassisted policy with a feedback-informed self-teacher, yet the teacher evolves with the student, creating unstable targets and motivating additional regularization. We introduce Function-Space Policy Optimization (FSPO), a single-policy framework that combines current privileged adaptation with function-space temporal consolidation. FSPO stores sparse historical next-token distributions as fixed temporal targets, providing temporal separation without maintaining a persistent teacher model. It further introduces privileged disagreement correction to explicitly suppress locally overvalued actions, reliability-adaptive grounding that strengthens reference supervision when self-generated evidence repeatedly fails, and quality and coverage-aware temporal memory that retains verified behaviors and improves privileged demonstrations. Across reasoning and tool-use benchmarks, FSPO achieves the highest average accuracy under a 5-hour training budget, improving over the strongest baseline by approximately 4% points on average while reducing peak memory from about 70 GB to 56 GB on Olmo3-7B-Instruct.
